lead: A CNC controller is the computer that turns a part program into real slide motion. It reads one block, works out the intermediate points along the wanted path, sends a position command to every axis, measures where the slide actually is, and keeps driving until the two agree. Without the controller the machine is only a set of motors; with it, the same hardware can cut a straight line, an arc or a free-form die cavity. Every CNC lathe and machining centre in a job shop runs this loop thousands of times a second.
prereq: You need: 6.2 for the feed drive, ball screw and guideways, and 6.1 for how the part program reaches memory.

blocks.text: A CNC controller is a computer with one special duty: keep several axes in step while also running the machine's housekeeping. The cabinet holds the usual PC parts plus dedicated boards for motion and for input/output.

The CPU runs the part program block by block (block syntax is in 6.4). Program memory stores the program and the tool offset table. The interpolator, usually software in the CPU, converts one block into a stream of position commands, one number per axis.

The PLC (programmable logic controller) is a second, separate processor for machine logic: coolant pump, tool changer, spindle orientation, door interlock, chip conveyor and alarm lamps. Motion and logic stay apart because motion must be smooth and on time, while a tool change is slow and event-driven.

The servo interface turns each position command into a signal the drive accepts: a pulse train, a ±10 V analogue demand, or a message on a digital fieldbus. The operator panel carries the display, jog keys, feed and spindle override, and the handwheel (MPG) used for setting up.

sections.h3: Three control systems and the loops inside them

items: Point-to-point: the axes move one at a time and only the final position matters. Drilling and punching tables work this way; the path between holes is irrelevant, so the machine can move fast.
Straight-cut (paraxial): the tool cuts along one axis at a controlled feed, or at 45° by pulsing two axes at the same rate. Used for simple rectangular milling.

Contouring (continuous path): two or more axes move together and the tool must stay on the wanted curve at every instant. Profiles, die cavities and turned tapers all need this, and it needs an interpolator.

blocks.text: Open loop means no measurement of the slide. A stepper motor turns a fixed angle per pulse and the controller trusts it. Cheap, but a heavy cut or a fast move can make it miss steps, and the error is never seen. Open loop is not 'no feedback from the program' — the program is followed in both types.

Closed loop means an encoder on the slide reports real position. The comparator subtracts feedback from the command and the leftover error drives the amplifier. Three loops nest: the current loop (fastest, controls motor torque), the velocity loop (tacho or differentiated encoder), and the position loop (outermost). The following error is the small lag between the commanded position and the measured position while the axis is moving; the position loop gain sets how large it is allowed to be.

A reference-pulse (incremental) interpolator outputs one pulse per basic length unit (BLU) on each axis. Pulse frequency sets the feed, and a counter converts pulses into position. It is simple and needs no feedback in an open-loop machine, and it suits stepper and older DC drives. Its limit is the pulse rate the counter and drive can accept.

A reference-word (absolute, sampled) interpolator does its arithmetic once every sample period T, typically 1 ms to 10 ms. Each axis receives a position word — 'be at 41.27 mm now'. The comparator subtracts the encoder count and the servo closes the loop. Modern AC servo machines work this way.

Linear interpolation finds the intermediate points on a straight line; circular interpolation finds them on an arc. The DDA (digital differential analyser) does both with adders: each axis holds an increment, adds it every iteration, and the carry-out becomes a pulse.

blocks.where: f is the pulse frequency along the path (pulses/s); v is the feed rate (mm/min); BLU is the basic length unit, the distance moved per pulse (mm); 60 converts minutes to seconds.
e is the chord error, the largest gap between the true arc and the straight chord (mm); L is the chord length (mm); R is the arc radius (mm). Small L and large R make e negligible.

sections.h3: Measuring the slide and checking the part

blocks.text: An incremental encoder has a slotted disc, a light source and a photocell. Channels A and B are 90° out of phase, and direction comes from which channel leads. Counting both edges of both channels gives four counts per grating line, so a 2500-line encoder yields 10 000 counts per revolution. A third Z channel marks one position per revolution for homing.

An absolute encoder reads a coded pattern and knows its position at power-on, so no homing is needed. A linear grating (glass scale) is fixed to the table and reads position directly, so screw pitch error and backlash stay outside the loop. A resolver is a small rotary transformer, rugged and analogue, still found on older machines.
A laser interferometer measures true distance along an axis to a fraction of a micrometre. It is used to check positioning accuracy and to fill the pitch-error compensation table inside the control.

For the part itself, a touch probe held in the spindle finds an edge or a bore and reports to the control; a coordinate measuring machine checks finished parts in a metrology room; in-process gauging measures during grinding and feeds the size back to the control.

examples.question: A CNC milling centre has a basic length unit (resolution) of 0.01 mm. One block commands a straight line from P0 (0, 0) to P1 (60, 40) mm at a feed rate of 1200 mm/min. Using a reference-pulse interpolator, find (a) the path length, (b) the machining time, and (c) the pulse rate on the X and Y axes.
steps: Machining time: t = L / v = 72.11 / 1200 = 0.06009 min = 3.606 s.
Pulses needed on X: 60 / 0.01 = 6000 pulses. On Y: 40 / 0.01 = 4000 pulses.
Check: the resultant pulse rate is √(1664² + 1109²) = √(2768896 + 1229881) = √3998777 ≈ 2000 pulses/s, which matches f = v / (60 × BLU) = 1200 / (60 × 0.01) = 2000 pulses/s.
examples.answer: Path length 72.11 mm, machining time 3.606 s, X pulse rate 1664 pulses/s and Y pulse rate 1109 pulses/s.
examples.check:
import math
L = math.hypot(60, 40)
t = L / 1200 * 60
xr = round(6000 / t)
yr = round(4000 / t)
print(round(L, 2))
print(round(t, 3))
print(xr)
print(yr)

traps: Open loop means no measurement of the slide, not 'no feedback from the program'. The part program drives both open-loop and closed-loop machines.
Quadrature gives four counts per grating line, not one. A 2500-line encoder on a 5 mm-pitch screw gives 5 / 10 000 = 0.0005 mm per count, not 0.002 mm.
Feed in mm/min and pulse rate in pulses/s differ by a factor of 60. Forgetting the 60 puts the answer out sixty times.
In point-to-point control the path is not controlled, so you cannot ask for the distance travelled between holes — only the final positions matter.
The chord error is L²/(8R), not L²/(2R). Work one numerical case with R = 50 mm and L = 1 mm to fix the factor 8 in your memory: e = 2.5 µm.

quiz.q: Name the two processors inside a CNC controller and state what each handles.
quiz.a: The CPU runs the part program and the interpolator. The PLC runs machine logic: coolant, tool change, door interlock and lamps.

quiz.q: Why does an open-loop machine lose position after a heavy cut while a closed-loop machine does not?
quiz.a: The stepper is trusted to follow every pulse, so a step lost under load is never seen or corrected. A closed-loop machine measures the slide with an encoder and the comparator keeps driving until the error falls to zero.

quiz.q: Feed rate 900 mm/min, BLU 0.005 mm. Find the pulse frequency along the path.
A 2500-line incremental encoder is coupled directly to a 5 mm-pitch ball screw and read in quadrature. Find the resolution in mm per count.
quiz.a: Counts per revolution = 4 × 2500 = 10 000. Resolution = 5 / 10 000 = 0.0005 mm per count.

quiz.q: An arc of radius 50 mm is cut as chords of 1 mm length. Find the chord error.
Contouring needs each axis to be given a new coordinated position at every instant, while point-to-point does not. Explain.
quiz.a: In point-to-point the path between holes does not matter, so each axis can simply run to its target and stop. In contouring the tool must be at the right point of the curve at every instant, so the controller must issue a fresh coordinated position for all axes at a fixed rate, and the servo must reach it before the next one arrives.

quiz.q: Give one reason to fit a linear scale instead of a rotary encoder on the screw.
quiz.a: The scale reads table position directly, so screw pitch error, backlash and thermal growth of the screw stay outside the loop.

quiz.q: What does a laser interferometer measure on a machine tool?
quiz.a: The true distance moved along an axis to very fine resolution; it is used to check positioning accuracy and to build the pitch-error compensation table.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production controllers now add look-ahead: they read many blocks ahead and slow the feed smoothly before a tight corner, so the machine never overshoots. Jerk-limited trajectory planning replaces the plain trapezoidal velocity profile. High-end controls interpolate NURBS curves directly instead of breaking them into tiny lines. Open-architecture controllers put the motion software on a PC talking to drives over a fieldbus, so the interpolator can be retuned or replaced. Search 'look-ahead trajectory planning', 'jerk-limited motion profile' and 'open architecture CNC' to go further.
